newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian banking sector fate linked to Royale Belge.
newsitem.headline: Belgian banking sector fate linked to Royale Belge.

text.p: The future of Belgian insurer Royale Belge hangs in the balance and with it the prospects for many of Belgium's financial services sector companies, analysts said on Tuesday.
There was intense speculation ahead of Royale Belge's annual shareholders meeting on Wednesday that the company, and its 12.4 percent stake in BBL, was about to be sold by French parent AXA-UAP.
"It has implications, not only for Royale Belge, but for Banque Bruxelles Lambert and if BBL, the question is what happens to Generale Bank," one analyst at a large Belgian bank said.
One newspaper cited Dutch financial services group ING and Swiss insurer Winterthur as suitors.
Winterthur denied the report and AXA-UAP and ING declined to comment.

BBL, Belgium's third largest bank, has been looking for an alliance for nearly two years. Plans last year to set up a Belgian banking giant with Generale Bank, Belgium's leading lender, were blocked by ING, a significant BBL minority shareholder.

A Royale Belge sale to ING would leave the Dutch group incontestably in control of BBL -- something it first aimed for in 1992 but failed to achieve. And that would put Generale Bank under enormous pressure to consolidate its own position.

While some analysts doubt the ING scenario -- and most now no longer expect a major announcement on Wednesday after Royale Belge last week cooled expectations -- the picture remains sufficiently cloudy for the heady speculation to go on for some time yet, they said.
The decision by French groups AXA and UAP last year to merge left AXA-UAP with two separate Belgian units, Royale Belge and AXA Belgium, a situation the group appears unhappy with.
At the presentation of 1996 results in March, AXA Belgium said a merger with Royale Belge appeared the "natural scenario" to remedy the situation. Feasibility studies were underway.
Analysts believe the merger idea has now been dropped, although the formal position of both companies is that all options remain open.

"A merger is possible but from an operational point of view it does not make much sense. You would get a bigger life insurance company but not many cost reductions or economies of scale," KB Securities analyst Dirk Peeters said.
The apparent mismatch has only served to heighten belief in some quarters that a divorce between Royale Belge or AXA Belgium and its parent is on the cards.
What does happen, analysts said, probably depends, as does much in the Belgian corporate world, on the plans of reclusive financier Albert Frere, the head of Belgium's Groupe Bruxelles Lambert.
GBL owns 25.1 percent of Royale Vendome, an intermediate holding company between AXA-UAP and Royale Belge. GBL also owns a direct stake of around 12.4 percent of BBL.

"My guess is the solution AXA-UAP would probably prefer is to buy out GBL and stay in Royale Belge," one analyst said, noting Royale Belge was a very profitable company in a life insurance market that was still growing.

KB Securities' Peeters said it was too early to speculate on Royale Belge's future without knowing Frere's intentions. Frere might want Royale Belge to first sell its BBL shares before he himself sold out of the insurer, he said.

Another factor in the future of BBL and the complicated cross-holdings that bind the various groups together is a European Commission inquiry into a shareholder pact set up between Royale Belge, GBL and Belgium's second largest bank Dexia CC. Together the three own around 37 percent of BBL, outvoting ING.
The Commission has so far not said whether it believes the pact should be scrapped or what changes it wants.
